P4c: At a federation level, that outward purpose gets concrete. I see the need to spread healing practices, train people and seed new projects. It's also important to keep any one comfortable enclave from forgetting that it isn't the whole movement.
P6c: On a related point, cooperation also shouldn't quietly turn into merging. The FEC has full members and communities working towards becoming full members, and it also has Friends who may simply stay friends. People need the same practical freedom of movement between communities. Somebody can be free to move in theory, but if their housing, status, health coverage, records, labor accounting, travel costs, taxes and transition disputes all fall through the cracks, that freedom's just decorative. A thin interface can often do it, one that says who's responsible for what while somebody crosses between them, without every community's internal systems having to match.
P6d: On a related point, cooperation also shouldn't quietly turn into merging. The FEC has full members and communities working towards becoming full members, and it also has Friends who may simply stay friends. People need the same practical freedom of movement between communities. In theory anyone can move. In practice, if housing, status, health coverage, records, labor accounting, travel costs, taxes and disputes over the transition fall through the cracks, the freedom is just decorative. What often works is a thin interface between communities that says who's responsible for what while somebody crosses between them. Their internal systems don't all have to match.
P8c: And when two principles collide and you make a rule out of it, store not only the resulting rule but also the original hard case: what happened, which principles were involved, what the first judgments were, what was finally decided and why, whether anyone dissented, what the consequences were, and which version of the rule it was decided under. When the rule changes, re-run the case. Otherwise each generation gets to rediscover the same constitutional fight from scratch.
P8d: When making a rule out of a collision between two principles, store not only the rule you end up with but also the original hard case, including which principles were involved, what judgments were made at first, what was finally decided and why, if there was any dissent, what the consequences were, and which version of the rule it was decided under. When the rule changes, re-run the case. Otherwise every generation gets to rediscover the same constitutional fight from scratch.
